case_study_insert.main_stem: Brightvolt EV Charging (BEC) is a public limited company in the electric vehicle charging sector, employing a workforce of 210. Founded in 2016 by Ada Mensah, the company operates 340 fast-charging bays across motorway service areas and retail parks, with a hierarchical structure and delegated regional management teams. BEC plans to invest $2,400,000 in nine 350 kW ultra-fast charging hubs along the M4 corridor, financed by a $1,500,000 share issue and a $900,000 five-year bank loan. It has fixed costs of $1,575,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $18, and currently produces 260,000 units a year. BEC faces a skills gap: its field technicians lack the high-voltage certification needed to commission the new hubs.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — October 2026: A survey of 800 motorway drivers found 57% prefer chargers offering 350 kW speeds, and 63% would pay $3 more per session for guaranteed bay availability. Average charging spend is $18 per session, with an average dwell time of 22 minutes. Website visits rose 48% after the spring influencer campaign. Customer complaints averaged 19 per month, down from 27. An internal audit found 9 of 210 field technicians lack high-voltage certification (off-the-job training at the specialist academy costs $1,600 per technician; on-the-job training is unsafe for live high-voltage work).

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Brightvolt EV Charging for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.7% from $12.40 to $13.23 per hour from April 2026, raising staff costs. (2) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.5% to 6.0%, the third rise this year, increasing borrowing costs. (3) Wholesale grid electricity costs for charging operators have risen 13.6% year-on-year, while electric-vehicle registrations grew 18.2% in the same period.

questions.question_text: BEC plans to finance the M4 charging hubs with a $1,500,000 share issue and a $900,000 five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for BEC of using the share issue instead of relying solely on bank borrowing.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $1,500,000 share issue raises permanent capital with no compulsory repayment schedule or interest, strengthening BEC's balance sheet while it carries fixed costs of $1,575,000 a year and a new $900,000 bank loan. The $2,400,000 hub programme can therefore proceed without over-stretching cash flow, and shareholders rather than lenders absorb the construction-phase risk before the nine 350 kW hubs open. Avoiding further lender covenants also keeps BEC free to direct operating cash into 350 kW hardware and software rather than accelerated repayments.

Point 2: Issuing shares spreads ownership risk across many investors and avoids the restrictive covenants and asset charges that a pure bank loan would attach to the charging estate. For a public limited company, a well-received share issue can also lift BEC's profile with the investment community, supporting the 18.2% growth in electric-vehicle registrations behind its market, and keeps Ada Mensah's strategy free from lender interference when choosing hub locations, pricing and rollout pace along the M4 corridor.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to Brightvolt EV Charging and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: BEC is launching its nine ultra-fast M4 charging hubs. Consider motorway service-area advertising, a national television campaign, or an EV-manufacturer partnership marketing programme. Which should BEC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Motorway service-area advertising: Advertising inside services on the M4 places BEC directly in front of drivers just as they approach range anxiety, with dwell time to absorb the message. It targets the 57% of 800 surveyed drivers who prefer 350 kW speeds and the 63% who would pay $3 more per session for guaranteed bay availability. Costs are far below national TV, and site-specific offers can be tracked. However, reach is limited to M4 users, other motorway corridors see nothing, and competitor hubs sit in the same services, so share of voice is contested.

National television campaign: TV would build mass brand awareness for Brightvolt across the UK driving public, positioning the nine hubs as a national fast-charging standard and supporting the share issue story. However, production and airtime costs run into hundreds of thousands of dollars — hard to justify while $2,400,000 is committed to hubs and $900,000 of bank debt is outstanding — and much of the audience will never drive the M4 corridor, wasting spend for marginal incremental sessions.

EV-manufacturer partnership marketing: Co-marketing with EV makers — in-car navigation prompts, onboarding packs and dealer referrals — reaches BEC's exact target at the moment of vehicle purchase, when charging habits are formed. It locks in high-value 350 kW users with manufacturer endorsement and measurable referral volumes, and the revenue from guaranteed $3 premium sessions improves the economics. Drawbacks are dependence on partner priorities, revenue-share negotiations, and slower brand independence.

Recommendation: BEC should choose EV-manufacturer partnership marketing. It reaches qualified ultra-fast drivers at the cheapest effective cost, converts the 57% who want 350 kW speeds into hub users, and builds durable volume that underwrites the share issue and loan. Motorway service-area advertising is rejected as the sole strategy because reach ends at one corridor and competition for attention is fierce; the national television campaign is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted while $2,400,000 is locked in hubs. BEC should layer low-cost service-area signage onto the manufacturer programme to catch corridor traffic.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of BEC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of BEC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why service-area advertising and television are rejected as lead strategies.

questions.question_text: BEC faces a skills gap, with 9 of 210 field technicians lacking high-voltage certification. Explain two benefits for BEC of using performance-related bonuses to motivate technicians to complete the certification.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Performance-related bonuses reward technicians who pass the high-voltage audit and complete the $1,600 academy course, satisfying esteem needs and making certification personally valuable. Linking bonuses to commissioning the nine M4 hubs on schedule focuses effort on the exact bottleneck delaying hub openings, so BEC converts its $2,400,000 investment into revenue faster.

Point 2: Bonuses tied to hub uptime, first-time-fix rates and complaint reduction (already improved from 27 to 19 per month) align pay with customer outcomes that motorway drivers notice — the 57% who want 350 kW speeds expect reliable bays. This raises certified capacity, lowers emergency-call costs, strengthens the 18.2% EV-registration tailwind behind BEC's market and protects its $18 selling price and $10.50 contribution per unit. Certified technicians also unlock safer unsupervised hub operation, which is essential once nine hubs open along the M4 corridor and delegated regional managers cannot supervise every site personally.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BEC's skills gap, hub launch and customer outcomes.

questions.question_text: BEC must appoint managers for the nine new M4 hubs. Consider internal promotion of existing operations staff or external recruitment of hub managers. Which should BEC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Internal promotion: Promoting BEC's own operations staff into hub manager roles rewards loyalty, strengthens morale and signals a clear career path in a 210-person workforce, supporting retention when high-voltage skills are scarce. Internal appointees already know the charging management system, service-area partners and safety rules, so the nine hubs open faster with less induction. However, BEC's bench of high-voltage-certified supervisors is thin — only part of the 9 uncertified audit group is promotable — and promoting before certification completes risks putting unqualified staff in safety-critical charge.

External recruitment of hub managers: External hires bring high-voltage commissioning experience, fresh network-operator contacts and relieve internal bottlenecks immediately; salaries and agency fees are higher, and new managers still need cultural induction into BEC's delegated regional model and Ada Mensah's customer-experience standards. Poorly chosen external hires could clash with service-area hosts or demotivate internal candidates who expected promotion.

Decision: BEC should choose internal promotion for most hub manager posts, with one or two external hires only where no certified internal candidate exists. Internal promotion is faster, cheaper and motivating across the 210-person workforce, leverages existing service-area relationships, and keeps Ada Mensah's standards consistent across the M4; it also complements the bonus scheme driving certification. External-first recruitment is rejected as costlier and culturally riskier as a general approach, though BEC should use external search selectively if certified internal candidates cannot cover all nine hubs. In all cases every hub manager, promoted or hired, must hold current high-voltage certification before commissioning, and external hires should still complete BEC's high-voltage audit before solo supervision.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two recruitment options with limited application to BEC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both recruitment options in the context of BEC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of BEC with a well-justified decision covering cost, speed, morale and certification.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how BEC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $1,575,000 ÷ ($18 − $7.50) = $1,575,000 ÷ $10.50 = 150,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 150,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $18 − $7.50 = $10.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $10.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways BEC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. BEC can compare its 150,000-unit break-even output with production of 260,000 units to confirm the current network is profitable, with a margin of safety of 110,000 units, giving confidence that nine additional hubs can be absorbed without losses at launch.
2. Contribution per unit of $10.50 lets BEC model the $3 premium for guaranteed bay availability: guaranteed sessions would earn $13.50 contribution, so managers can forecast how many premium sessions per hub pay back the premium bay-reservation system investment.
3. Contribution data lets managers check the expansion is bankable: each M4 hub must cover a share of fixed costs of $1,575,000 a year and the $900,000 five-year bank loan, so pricing, utilisation targets and the guaranteed-availability product can be tied to repayment schedules.
4. Unit cost data ($1,575,000 ÷ 260,000 units + $7.50 = $13.56 a unit) helps managers benchmark hub performance, identify the waste behind the 19 complaints per month and 22-minute dwell times, and negotiate electricity supply contracts as grid power costs rise 13.6%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 150,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $10.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 110,000 units vs 260,000-unit output; premium-bay pricing modelling; loan-repayment feasibility for the $2,400,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at $13.56 for electricity and service control.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate BEC's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has BEC's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 47.5%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 figures ($'000): gross profit $1,560,000 ÷ revenue $3,900,000 × 100 = 40.0%; 2025: gross profit $2,223,000 ÷ revenue $4,680,000 × 100 = 47.5%. Operating profit against revenue: 2024: $468,000 ÷ $3,900,000 × 100 = 12.0%; 2025: $702,000 ÷ $4,680,000 × 100 = 15.0%. Operating profit against capital employed: 2024: $468,000 ÷ $2,600,000 × 100 = 18.0%; 2025: $702,000 ÷ $3,510,000 × 100 = 20.0%. Cost of sales grew from $2,340,000 to $2,457,000 but fell from 60.0% to 52.5% of revenue, while capital employed expanded from $2,600,000 to $3,510,000 as the M4 investment entered the balance sheet; interest payable rose from $165,000 to $210,000.

Evaluation: Profitability has improved robustly. Revenue grew 20.0% from $3,900,000 to $4,680,000, consistent with 260,000 units and an 18.2% rise in EV registrations. Gross profit surged from 40.0% to 47.5%, reflecting better electricity procurement, pricing power on the $18 session price and growing premium $3 guaranteed-bay revenue. Operating profit improved from 12.0% to 15.0%, showing overheads were absorbed despite rapid expansion; the rise in interest payable to $210,000 signals growing leverage on the $900,000 loan. Operating profit against capital employed rose from 18.0% to 20.0% — capital is being deployed effectively even with the asset base growing 35.0%. Caution: the 13.6% grid electricity cost rise could erode the 47.5% gross figure in 2026 if tariffs are not passed through, and the M4 launch must convert pipeline interest from the spring influencer campaign (+48% website visits) into plug-in sessions.

Conclusion: BEC's financial performance has improved. Gross profit (40.0% to 47.5%), operating profit against revenue (12.0% to 15.0%) and operating profit against capital employed (18.0% to 20.0%) all rose, backed by 20.0% revenue growth. BEC should lock in these gains through off-peak electricity contracts and the guaranteed-bay premium, and ensure the nine hubs are commissioned with certified technicians so returns do not stall.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, operating profit and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether BEC's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for BEC of introducing contactless payment technology at all its charging hubs.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Contactless payment removes the need for membership cards and apps at the 340 existing bays and nine new hubs, cutting queues and dwell time friction for the 63% who would pay $3 more for guaranteed bay availability. Faster transactions raise throughput per bay, support the 22-minute average dwell, and provide clean transaction data that BEC can reuse in its spring influencer campaigns (website visits already rose 48%) to target repeat customers. It also matches the contactless habits EV drivers bring from retail and fuel purchases, lowering the adoption barrier for first-time hub users.

Disadvantage: Contactless terminals add hardware, transaction fees and payment-security duties to every bay, adding to the $1,575,000 fixed costs and to the $2,400,000 hub capex programme. Outages or declined cards at nine brand-new M4 sites would strand paying drivers and push complaints back above 27 per month, damaging the brand precisely when BEC needs word-of-mouth to fill the hubs; BEC must also keep fallback payment routes for drivers whose cards fail in high-voltage environments.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BEC's operations, finances and customers.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the 6.7% minimum wage increase to $13.23, the interest rate rise to 6.0% and the 13.6% rise in grid electricity costs will affect BEC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Minimum wage increase (6.7%, to $13.23 per hour): With a workforce of 210, mainly field technicians and site staff, a 6.7% rise adds roughly $1,750 per employee a year, or about $367,000 across the workforce — very significant against 2025 operating profit of $702,000. BEC must lift productivity (260,000 units ÷ 210 staff ≈ 1,238 units per employee), use the bonus scheme to reward certified work, and prioritise high-impact retention measures for high-voltage technicians rather than applying flat rises.

Interest rate rise (5.5% to 6.0%): BEC's $900,000 five-year bank loan becomes costlier by roughly $4,500 a year per 0.5 percentage points, pushing interest payable above the $210,000 already recorded in Appendix 2. The share issue funds most of the M4 build, so direct exposure is limited, but a higher base rate also cools housing and car-buying sentiment and could dampen EV registrations, and refinancing after five years will be more expensive if rates stay high. The cash impact is manageable and manageable through fixing rates.

Grid electricity cost rise (13.6%): Electricity is the fuel inside BEC's $7.50 variable cost per unit. A 13.6% rise adds roughly $0.70–$0.90 per unit; across 260,000 units a year that is $180,000–$235,000 a year, dragging contribution from $10.50 toward $9.60–$9.80 and squeezing exactly the margin that justifies $2,400,000 of M4 hubs. Unlike wages, this cost recurs on every single unit sold and cannot be fully delegated to staff productivity.

Conclusion: The 13.6% rise in grid electricity costs will have the greatest impact. It scales directly with volume (260,000 units), totalling roughly $180,000–$235,000 a year, and attacks the $10.50 contribution margin on which the entire nine-hub M4 business case rests. The minimum wage rise is the second-largest, at around $367,000 across 210 staff, while the interest rate rise is smallest in cash terms and can be hedged by fixing the $900,000 loan; BEC should respond with off-peak PPAs, dynamic pricing, the $3 guaranteed-bay premium and rigorous site productivity.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to BEC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on BEC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of BEC with a well-justified judgment that the electricity cost rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
